LEV_DEQ.instruction: Keep the cells that are waiting to be explored in a first-in-first-out queue (collections.deque, taking cells from the left end) and always take the cell that has been waiting the longest.
LEV_DEQ.instruction_round3: Process cells strictly in the order they were discovered, using collections.deque with popleft().

LEV_HEAP.instruction: Keep the frontier in a binary heap (heapq) whose priority is the number of steps from the start cell, with ties broken by an insertion counter, and always pop the cell with the fewest steps.
LEV_HEAP.instruction_round3: Use heapq with entries (steps_from_start, counter, cell); pop the smallest entry each time.

LEV_SET.instruction: Keep the current ring of cells (all cells the same number of steps from the start) in a Python set; from it build the next ring as a new set of unvisited free neighbours, then replace the current ring with the new one, and repeat.
LEV_SET.instruction_round3: Advance a whole ring of cells at a time: the frontier is a set of cells at distance d, and the next frontier is the set of their new free neighbours at distance d + 1.

LEV_ARR.instruction: Use no queue, stack or heap: keep a 2-D distance grid, give the start distance 0, and for d = 0, 1, 2, ... scan the whole grid for cells whose distance is d and give each of their unlabelled free neighbours distance d + 1; stop when the goal gets a distance or a scan labels nothing, then walk back from the goal along decreasing distances.
LEV_ARR.instruction_round3: Label distances on a 2-D list: on pass d, look at every cell of the grid and, for each cell labelled d, label its unlabelled free neighbours d + 1; no frontier container at all.

DFS_STK.instruction: Use a stack (a Python list with append and pop() from the end) or recursion, always continuing from the most recently discovered cell so that the search goes as deep as possible before it backs up.
DFS_STK.instruction_round3: Explore with a last-in-first-out stack held in a Python list (append / pop()), or with a recursive helper, always extending the newest cell first.

DFS_DEQ.instruction: Keep the frontier in a collections.deque but use only its right end: append new cells on the right and take the next cell with pop() from the right.
DFS_DEQ.instruction_round3: Use collections.deque as a last-in-first-out structure: append() to add and pop() to remove, never popleft().

DFS_HEAP.instruction: Keep the frontier in a heapq heap whose priority is the negative of an insertion counter, so the most recently added cell is always popped first.
DFS_HEAP.instruction_round3: Use heapq with entries (-counter, cell) where counter increases with every push, so the newest cell comes out first.

HEU_HEAP.instruction: Keep the frontier in a heapq heap whose priority is the Manhattan distance from the cell to the goal (optionally plus the number of steps taken so far), and always pop the cell with the smallest priority.
HEU_HEAP.instruction_round3: Use heapq with entries whose first element is the Manhattan distance to the goal (you may add the steps so far) and pop the smallest entry each time.

HEU_SLIST.instruction: Keep the frontier as a Python list that stays sorted by the Manhattan distance to the goal (insert (key, counter, cell) tuples with bisect.insort) and always take the first element of the list.
HEU_SLIST.instruction_round3: Maintain a Python list in ascending order of the Manhattan distance to the goal using bisect.insort, and remove the first element each step.

HEU_ARR.instruction: Use no queue, stack, heap or sorted list: keep a 2-D grid of open flags; at each step scan the whole grid for the open cell with the smallest Manhattan distance to the goal (ties by row, then column), close it, and open its unvisited free neighbours.
HEU_ARR.instruction_round3: Without any frontier container, keep 2-D boolean arrays of open and closed cells and, each step, scan every cell to find the open one nearest to the goal by Manhattan distance.

RLX_ARR.instruction: Use no queue, stack or heap: keep a 2-D distance grid (0 at the start, infinity elsewhere) and repeat full sweeps over the grid in row-major order, setting each free cell's distance to one plus the smallest neighbour distance whenever that is smaller, until a sweep changes nothing; then walk back from the goal along decreasing distances.
RLX_ARR.instruction_round3: Compute distances by repeated full passes over a 2-D array (row by row, column by column), lowering each free cell's value to one more than its smallest neighbour, until a pass makes no change.

RLX_STK.instruction: Keep a worklist stack (a Python list with append and pop() from the end) and a distance table; whenever a cell's tentative distance improves, record the new distance and push the cell again, even if it was processed before; stop when the stack is empty, then rebuild the path from the goal with parent links.
RLX_STK.instruction_round3: Use a Python list as a last-in-first-out worklist of cells to re-examine; a cell is pushed every time its distance label drops, including cells that were already popped before.

RLX_HEAP.instruction: Keep a worklist in a heapq heap ordered by the cell's (row, col), not by distance; pop the cell with the smallest (row, col), and whenever a neighbour's tentative distance improves, record it and push that neighbour again, even if it was processed before; continue until the heap is empty, then rebuild the path from parent links.
RLX_HEAP.instruction_round3: Use heapq as a worklist ordered by the tuple (row, col); every time a cell's distance label drops, push it again, including cells that were already popped before.

RND_HEAP.instruction: Keep the frontier in a heapq heap whose priority is a fresh random number (random.random()) drawn when the cell is added, and always pop the cell with the smallest random key.
RND_HEAP.instruction_round3: Use heapq with entries (random.random(), cell) so that frontier cells come out in random order.

RND_SET.instruction: Keep the frontier as a Python set and choose the next cell to explore with random.choice over the frontier (convert it to a tuple first), removing the chosen cell from the set.
RND_SET.instruction_round3: Hold the frontier in a set and, each step, take a uniformly random member with random.choice(tuple(frontier)).

CRD_HEAP.instruction: Keep the frontier in a heapq heap keyed only by the cell's coordinates (row, col), ignoring the goal and the number of steps, and always pop the cell with the smallest (row, col).
CRD_HEAP.instruction_round3: Use heapq with entries (row, col): the frontier cell with the smallest row (then column) is always explored next, whatever the goal is.

CRD_SLIST.instruction: Keep the frontier as a Python list that stays sorted by the cell's coordinates (row, then column) using bisect.insort, ignoring the goal and the number of steps, and always take the first element.
CRD_SLIST.instruction_round3: Keep the frontier in a list sorted with bisect.insort by (row, col) and always remove the first element, whatever the goal is.

PROBE.instruction: Use a label-correcting method: keep a first-in-first-out queue (collections.deque, taking cells from the left end) and a distance table; whenever a neighbour's tentative distance improves, update it and append that neighbour to the queue again, even if it was processed before; when the queue is empty, rebuild the path from parent links.
PROBE.instruction_round3: Keep a FIFO queue (collections.deque with popleft) of cells whose distance label dropped; re-append a cell every time its label drops, even after it has been processed.
